Ladies and gentlemen, it's time to start. I call to order the High-level Forum on the Programme of Action on a Culture of Peace. This meeting is held in accordance with resolution 79/321 of 25 July 2025, entitled follow up to the declaration and program of action on a culture of Peace as mentioned in my letters dated 8th and 20th August 2025 this meeting will consist of an opening segment and a plenary segment Your Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, I welcome you all to this high-level forum on a culture of peace. Allow me to take this opportunity to express my deep appreciation to the permanent mission of Bangladesh for its steadfast commitment to advancing the resolution on the program of action on a culture of peace. Your Excellencies, we convened this high-level meeting today under the theme of empowering youth for a culture of peace. This theme is both timely and significant. It resonates with Security Council Resolution 2550 of 2015, which affirm the vital role of young people in building and sustaining peace. It also reflects the vision of the Pact for the Future, which recognizes the important contributions youth are already making to the advancement of peace and security. Make no mistake, young people are not passive beneficiaries of peace. They are leaders, innovators, and agents of change. Empowering them is one of the most effective ways to ensure that a culture of peace takes root in every society and endures across generations. But that potential can only be realized if we listen to young people systematically and comprehensively, working alongside them to create meaningful opportunities for their future. Your Excellencies, across the globe, youth-led organizations and movements are underscoring the vital role in peace, tolerance, and dialogue. It is demonstrating that young people not only imagine a better world, they dedicate themselves to building it. Yet, in spite of the clear opportunities, many places such as Gaza, Haiti, Sudan and Ukraine, conflict and crisis continue to obstruct their efforts and undermine their potential. Your Excellencies, the barriers they face are clear. Too many lack access to quality education. Too many are marginalized by social norms. Too many are excluded from political decision-making. Indeed, in conflict zones, young people are often drawn into violence or fall victim to it, perpetuating cycles of instability. These realities make it urgent to take meaningful steps and to equip young people with the knowledge, resources and opportunities they need to participate fully in peacebuilding and conflict prevention. Your Excellencies, let us treat this forum as a call to action to build a world that is safe, peaceful, just, inclusive, sustainable, and prosperous. When young people learn the values of tolerance, empathy, and conflict resolution early in life, they carry those values into adulthood. This creates future generations with the skills to sustain peace. Education systems must integrate the values of peace, and governments must reflect on and support the transformative role that young people can play in creating more harmonious societies. As Nelson Mandela once urged, to the youth of today, I also have a wish to make. Be the scriptwriters of your destiny and feature yourselves as stars that show the way towards a brighter future. Thank you. I give the floor to Dr. Philippe Paulier, Assistant Secretary General for Youth Affairs.

Thank you very much.

Dear President of the General Assembly, distinguished delegates from several member states, and also partners in the room. It's my honor to join you for this high-level forum on the program of action on a culture of peace. And I'm very keen and happy to see that the focus of this forum is in the role and how we create spaces for empowerment of young people when we are promoting this agenda of a culture of peace. When the UN adopted the program of action in 1999, we affirmed as a global community that peace is not only the absence of war, but peace is the presence of justice, of dignity, of inclusion and the respect for future generations. 26 years later, this vision is more needed than ever. Inequalities are deepening, conflicts are multiplying. The President of the General Assembly was referring to some of the most painful situations we're facing as a global community. And trust in our institutions is eroding. But yet, you know, every time there's a space for young people, there's a door, there's a window we open for youth to engage with our global community. There's also hope, you know, hope carried by the 1.9 billion young people worldwide that are not only imagining a better world, but they are actively building it through solidarity, through innovation in the communities and beyond. Resolution 79321 adopted this July underscores the role of youth when it's about advancing peace, sustainable development and human rights. From countering violent extremism to mobilizing for climate justice, young people are demonstrating all of us that peace is a daily practice. But too often their contributions are celebrated in words, but yet they are not reflected in budgets. Because the truth is that youth-led initiatives, youth programs are underfunded. The voices of young people are still too rarely embedded into decision-making, as it was very clearly highlighted by the President of the General Assembly. So empowering youth for a culture of peace requires investment, requires trust and requires partnerships. The good thing is that there's good practices. I'm here with ASG Speher and I believe that the Peacebuilding Fund, it's a clear example of a good mechanism when it's about empowering young people where they actually are in the communities building sustainable peace and understanding that building peace, it's about the connections of the three pillars of this organization. And that's also why in my role as Assistant Secretary General for Youth, in the role of a recently established United Nations Youth Office, We are working very closely with DPPA, with UNFPA, with DPO, with the Office of Disarmament, with the UN Alliance of Civilizations, with UNODC, with UNDP, and with many other parts of the system when it's about promoting the youth peace and security agenda. And that's why also we're so committed to really understand that advancing a culture of peace is really advancing a culture of youth participation. And that's why our office launched this year with several partners within the UN system and beyond a new flagship initiative framed under this idea of a youth compass, a compass for young people when it's about navigating institutional participation, but also a compass for our institutions to really guide and solve the issues that are affecting young people globally. And that's why alongside the Pact for the Future, alongside the Youth 2030 Strategy of the UN, we are embedding youth leadership and we are promoting also more avenues to unlock funding for youth initiatives. Peace will endure only when youth are treated as equal partners, when we really engage young people as co architects of sustainable future. And building a culture of peace is about building classrooms free of hate. It's about building workplaces free of discrimination. It's about civic spaces that are open and public squares filled with dialogue instead of division. And it's about trust. And it's about how, as institutions, we really trust and we understand that young people are our partners to build a more peaceful and sustainable future. So as we open this forum, I hope that this is also an opportunity not only for strong declarations, but also for concrete commitments when it's about really investing, protecting and standing with young people as we chart pathways for peace for this and for future generations. Thank you very much, President.
I thank the Assistant Secretary-General for Youth Affairs. I give the floor to Ms. Elizabeth Merits-Peher, Assistant Secretary-General for Peacebuilding Support.

Thank you very much. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, I'd like to start by thanking the organizers and particularly His Excellency, the President of the General Assembly, Mr. Philemon Yeng, for convening us here today for this very important meeting. At the turn of the century, through resolution 53243, the General Assembly committed to a culture of peace through the building of societies based on justice, equity, and mutual respect. Today, this world remains to be built, while the vision remains essential. We meet at a time when violent conflict is at an historic high, and discord and divisions continue to erode trust within and between societies. The legacy that older generations are leaving to the younger is fraught. And as the world is faced with myriad challenges, not least a context where war and destruction have once again become privileged tools to address disputes, we can no longer afford to keep young people outside of the spheres of action or the realms of decision-making. Yet, global studies show that three in four young people feel unheard by their politicians. And more than 80% of young people surveyed in 65 countries confirmed that electoral violence was hindering their participation in democratic processes. At the same time that many young people feel alienated and shut out from peace policy and politics, they are bearing the brunt of conflict around the world. One in four young people worldwide face conflict, with the lack of opportunities for youth frequently driving their recruitment into armed groups. And alarmingly, over 90% of direct conflict deaths are young adult males. Despite these sobering realities, we have countless examples of young women and men around the globe who have stepped up. and our leading efforts to prevent violence by fostering dialogue, promoting tolerance, and countering the narratives of hate with narratives of hope. The commitment and creativity of these young people remind us that a culture of peace need not be a distant aspiration. Our youth is one of our most precious resources, and young women and men can and do contribute to peace But many continue to face major obstacles exclusion from policy and decision making fora, shrinking civic space and insufficient support for their efforts, as my colleague and friend Felipe also has mentioned. To help address this, the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs has strongly committed to the youth peace and security agenda and, through its peacebuilding support office, is working alongside the UN youth office, as well as UNFPA, as part of the UN youth peace and security secretariat. Allow me to outline three areas in which the department has been working to empower youth for the building of a culture of peace. Firstly, integrating young people into peace processes and programs. Secondly, investing in youth-focused and youth-led initiatives. And thirdly, promoting youth's vital role in sustaining peace and conflict prevention. Regarding the first point, last year, DPPA launched its first Youth Peace and Security Strategy aimed at supporting member states and regional organizations in institutionalizing the YPS agenda through action plans. In addition to country-level support, we've partnered with the League of Arab States and ASEAN on regional strategies for meaningful youth participation. Secondly, DPPA has consistently invested in youth-led initiatives, especially through the support of the Secretary-General's Peacebuilding Fund, empowering young people as equal partners and key drivers of peace. For example, in Mali, PBF investments helped improve youth livelihoods and supported a new national youth policy to build trust between community leaders and young people. In Colombia, young leaders have been playing a crucial role in transitional justice and reintegration efforts. In South Sudan, youth peace committees reduced communal violence in hard-to-reach areas. Across these diverse contexts, young people have been at the forefront of local peace action, embodying the preventive spirit of the Programme of Action on a Culture of Peace. Finally, DPPA contributes to YPS advocacy and showcasing the vital efforts of young peacemakers and peacebuilders around the world. In addition to its penholder role for the Secretary-General's reports on YPS, Action 20 of the Pact for the Future mandated a second independent progress study on youth, peace and security, which will be guided by DPPA-PBSO in close partnership with UNFPA and the UN Youth Office, informed by a series of regional consultations and presented at next year's 80th UN General Assembly. A first regional YPS consultation for the report has already taken place in February of this year. Over 300 youth and high-level stakeholders gathered in Addis Ababa, showcasing the growing momentum of the agenda as a vital tool for empowering young people to shape Africa's future. To finalize, I would highlight some key points and lessons learned that have emerged from this work and are relevant to today's discussion. First, Empowering youth to contribute to, and indeed to lead in building a culture of peace, will require investing more in capacity building and resourcing for youth-led organizations, with an emphasis on more flexible, localized funding. Second, we must strengthen diverse youth participation in the context of our work. Youth is not a monolithic block. While intersectional approaches take time and require conscientious planning, they are essential. Third, all Member States should be encouraged to co-create and implement national action plans on youth, peace and security together with young people as key partners, in order to strongly anchor the agenda in society and to ensure that youth is meaningfully included in shaping peace and security policies from the outset. Fourth, consideration should be given to establishing an annual Security Council meeting on YPS to ensure that youth inclusion receives the attention it deserves at the highest levels of multilateral decision-making. With the 2025 Peacebuilding Architecture Review, the 10th anniversary of Resolution 2250, and the 30th anniversary of the World Programme of Action for Youth, We have a unique opportunity to galvanize efforts around strong youth involvement to advance a much needed culture of peace. It's time to align global frameworks with local realities and fully integrate young people as active and powerful agents of change, innovation and peace leadership. Thank you.

I thank the Assistant Secretary General for Peacebuilding Support. And I give the floor to His Excellency Ambassador Anwarul Chowdhury, former Under-Secretary-General and High Representative of the United Nations and the founder of the Global Movement for the Culture of Peace.

Thank you, Mr. President. I am deeply honored and delighted to speak at this year's 14th UN High-Level Forum on the Culture of Peace. As the founder of the Global Movement for the Culture of Peace, popularly known as GMCoP, which is the vanguard civil society coalition advancing the culture of peace worldwide. Thank you, Mr. President, most sincerely for your warm invitation. I dedicate my remarks at this August high-level forum to my dear friend, collaborator and moral companion, erstwhile Director-General of UNESCO, Professor Federico Mayor Zaragoza, whom we lost last December in Madrid. Federico was more than a towering intellectual and a compassionate leader. He was the kind of human being whose presence carried both gravity and grace. Our paths converged through our shared belief in the transformative power of the culture of peace. not merely as a slogan or aspiration, but as a guiding principle for humanity's collective future. Federico was the first keynote speaker when the High Level Forum was launched in 2012. And since then, he honored the United Nations General Assembly by his inspirational presence and wisdom at all the annual forums till 2022. May his legacy encourage us to continue our determined movement for the culture of peace. With your kind concurrence, Mr. President, may this special gathering observe a moment of silence in honor of Federico Mayor Zaragoza's departed soul and noble memory. Thank you. Since 2012, when the first UN High-Level Forum was initiated by the 66th PGA Ambassador Nasir Al-Nasser. This day-long high-level forum is being convened annually by the Presidents of the General Assembly on or around 13 September, as mandated by the Assembly's own resolutions. On that date, In 1999, the United Nations took the most forward-looking stride aimed at ensuring a peaceful planet for all of us since the Charter of the United Nations in 1995. The UN Charter arose out of the ashes of the Second World War, and the UN Declaration and the Programme of Action on Culture of Peace emerged in the aftermath of the long-drawn Cold War. More than a quarter century has passed by since the adoption by consensus and without reservation a monumental document on the culture of peace. It was an honor for me to chair as the Bangladesh permanent representative the nine month long open-ended negotiations that led to the agreement of on this historic norm setting document. I introduced the agreed text of that document now resolution A/53/243 on behalf of all member states for adoption by the assembly with its president Didier Auperti of Uruguay chairing the meeting. This high level forum is very special in its involvement of civil society. It is the only platform in the UN which is fully 50/50 gender balanced in the panel compositions, as we observe at this afternoon's speakers list. The event is honored to feature six Nobel Peace Laureates out of its first 10 keynote speakers at the Culture of Peace forums. and I would say proudly that all of them are distinguished women Nobel laureates. In 2012, as the senior special advisor of the 66th PGA, I had the honor of planning the organizational and conceptual structure of this high level annual event. The core idea was to realize two basic guidelines set in the Culture of Peace Declaration, namely, and I quote them, "Governments have an essential role in promoting and strengthening a culture of peace." And the second one, "Civil society needs to be fully engaged in fuller development of a culture of peace." In subsequent years, I was the chair moderator of the forum's panel discussions, as well as an invited speaker during 11 UNGA sessions. In simple terms, the culture of peace as a concept means that every one of us needs to consciously make peace and nonviolence a part of our daily existence. We should not isolate peace as something separate or distant. We should know how to relate to one another without being aggressive, without being violent, without being disrespectful, without neglect and without prejudice. The programme of action identifies eight specific areas which encourages action at all levels, the individual, the family, the community, the nation, the region and of course the global level. The essence of the culture of peace is its message of self transformation and its message of inclusiveness, of global solidarity and of the oneness of humanity. For nearly three decades, my focus has been on advancing the culture of peace, which aims at making peace and nonviolence a part of our own self, our own personality. This has now become more pertinent amid the ever-increasing militarism militarization and weaponization that is destroying both our planet and our people. Let me share with you a very encouraging step forward for the culture of peace. In September 2021, invited by the president of the UN General Assembly, president of the organization called Mayors for Peace, Mr. Kazumi Matsui, the current mayor of Hiroshima, in his virtual participation at this high-level forum, announced that in July 2021, Mayors for Peace, with its more than 8,200 member cities in 160-plus countries, adopted its new vision to include the objective to promote the culture of peace, in addition to the two other ongoing objectives of a world without nuclear weapons and of safe and resilient cities. Mr. President, I would now identify four areas which constitute the way forward for the culture of peace in the coming years. Transformative education. Never has it been more important for us to learn about the world and understand its diversity. The task of educating children and young people to find non-aggressive means to relate with one another is of primary importance. All educational institutions need to offer opportunities that prepare the students not only to live fulfilling lives, but also to be responsible and productive citizens of the world. Indeed, such education for peace should be more appropriately called education for global citizenship. Such learning cannot be achieved without well-intentioned, sustained and systematic peace education that leads the way to the culture of peace. If our minds could be likened to a computer, then transformative education provides the software with which to reboot our priorities and actions for transition from force to reason, from conflict to dialogue. Number two, women. As I always say emphatically, and I quote my own quotation, "Without peace, development cannot be realized. Without development, peace is not achievable. But without women, neither peace nor development is conceivable. Number three, youth and children. It is essential to recognize the empowerment of young people as a major element in building the culture of peace. This forum's theme underscores that very strongly. Young people of today should embrace the culture of peace in a way that can not only shape their lives but also can shape the future of the world. For this, I believe that early childhood affords a window of opportunity for us to sow the seeds of transition to the culture of peace from an early life. I'm encouraged to find that this is the fourth time and the third even Secretary-General's Youth Envoy is participating at this forum. I am also congratulating Assistant Secretary-General for Peacebuilding Support Office for joining the forum for the second time. Finally, number four, on centrality of the United Nations engagement. Often I am asked how the UN is doing. in the implementation of the Programme of Action adopted in 1999, meaning that it was adopted 25 years ago. I believe that the Organization should own it and internalize its implementation throughout the UN system. Also, the Secretary-General should prioritize the culture of peace as a part of his or her leadership agenda, hopefully. He or she should make good use of this workable tool that UN possesses in the Culture of Peace Program to advance the objective of sustainable peace. Not using the tool of the Culture of Peace can be likened to a person who needs a car to go to work and has a car, but with a minimal interest in knowing how to drive it. Let me conclude, Mr. President, by asserting that the culture of peace is not a quick fix. It is a movement, not a revolution. The seed of peace exists in all of us, It must be nurtured, cared for and promoted by us all to flourish. Peace cannot be imposed from outside. It must be realized from within. Let us send a strong, loud and clear message from this forum that there is no place for war, violence, hatred, prejudice, and intolerance in our world. I thank you, Mr. President.
I thank Mr. Chowdhury. And I give the floor to Ms. Chantelle Marikira Chakara, founder of the Little Dreamers Foundation.

Thank you, Mr. President. The President of the UN General Assembly, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, colleagues, let me begin by asking you three simple questions. What good is economic growth if it collapses in the rubble of war? What good are schools If children must flee before they learn? And finally, what good are jobs if young people are conscripted into conflict instead of building their futures? That is the reality of our moment. Conflict is undoing decades of progress. In 2023 alone, violent conflict displaced 114 million people, and cost the global economy $17.5 trillion, which is approximately 13% of world GDP. Now, that shows you that peace is no longer a local concern. It is a global currency. And today, that currency is dangerously devalued. Centuries ago, Thomas Hobbes warned us what life would look like without peace. No industry, no culture, no learning, only fear and the continual danger of violent death. And yet, here's the other truth. With peace, everything else becomes possible. Schools flourish, markets grow, jobs multiply, and dignity and hope take root. I stand before you today, not as one voice alone, but as the voice of the world's 1.8 billion young people, the largest generation in history, a generation that's already mediating conflicts, building trust, and imagining futures where others see only despair. Yet our efforts remain largely invisible and unrecognized by many. The High Level Forum comes at a pivotal time. In July, the General Assembly adopted resolution 79/321, reaffirming the role of youth in advancing human rights, promoting sustainable development, and shaping peace.

But it also leaves us with a clear responsibility.

To ensure the full, effective, constructive, and inclusive participation of youth in decision making. This is not an abstract conversation.

The evidence is clear.

The progress study, the missing piece found that peace processes that include youth are 35% more likely to last at least 15 years. the Aman Youth Declaration, the Guiding Principles on Young People's Participation in Peacebuilding, and Security Council Resolutions 2250, 2419, and 2535, all affirm that youth participation, protection, prevention, partnership, and reintegration are the five pillars of sustainable peace. And make no mistake about it.

These are not youth issues alone.

They are development strategies in legal form directly tied to the sustainable development goals. When youth are included, reconciliation holds, investment returns, and societies grow. And yet, let us be honest, delivering speeches in these halls is not enough.

Passing resolutions is not enough.

Issuing declarations is simply not enough. What matters is what follows implementation, investment, and accountability. And here I must speak plainly. I'm tired of hearing, well, if you don't have a seat at the table, bring your own chair. Or, well, how about you build your own table then? No. Young people do not need another slogan about bringing our own chairs or building our own tables. We could do that if we wished, but no, a resounding no. How about for once you invite us in? And I do not mean tokenist representation, I mean partnership. Resource us, ask for our counsel, give us real roles. Make us part of your decision-making bodies because what we seek is not symbolism. We seek the opportunity to see this through. And let us be clear, denying youth a seat at the table is not just unfair, it's an outright failure of strategy. And if you give young people one such opportunity, we will transform it into a legacy of enduring consequence. one that transcends boundaries, binds generations, and bends history toward justice. Excellences, if we are serious about creating a culture of sustainable peace, then we must be serious about youth. That means moving from symbolic gestures to structural change. And here I offer three fundamental pillars that I believe to be crucial. Number one, institutionalize youth participation in governance and peace processes from national to international spaces. Number two, provide political, financial, technical, and logistical support for youth organizations that bridge divides and create livelihoods. And lastly, reform education with tailored age appropriate methods that teach employable skills and civic values. So the question before you today is simple. What will you choose? What will you choose? Will you choose to let peace remain underfunded, youth underrepresented, and progress reversible, or will you choose to change the course of history? I know as statesmen and leaders, you may have your differences, different histories, different priorities, and even different visions of the path ahead. But I also know this, I believe in the power of this body to do what is right for humanity. I believe in the wisdom of each of you and in the courage that has brought you to this assembly. So I ask you this afternoon, act not with words alone, but with commitments, with resources, with the political will to empower.

Youth for a culture of peace.

Because if you do, history will look back on this moment and say, they chose wisely. They chose courageously. They chose peace. And they built the foundation for everything else. Thank you.

I thank Ms. Chakara. We have heard the last speaker in the opening segment. We will pause the meeting briefly to allow our speakers to leave the podium. We will now begin the plenary segment. Mr. President, Excellencies, distinguished delegates, it is my honor to deliver this statement on behalf of Bangladesh at this year's high-level forum convened under the theme, empowering youth for a culture of peace. We express our deep appreciation to the President of the General Assembly for this timely initiative. We also thank all the distinguished speakers for their insightful contributions. Excellencies, For over two decades, the landmark resolution on culture of peace adopted by the General Assembly, an initiative tabled by Bangladesh, has been reminding us that peace, compassion, mutual respect, and solidarity are not just idols. They are imperatives for empowering humanity. The call for a culture of peace has become more relevant than ever in the context of our current realities, When violence is often justified in the name of self-defense, hate speech spreads faster than dialogue. And who can champion this cause better than our youth? With their creativity and perseverance, young people are uniquely placed to carry forward this torch. The enormous potential of more than one billion young people globally must be harnessed effectively for ensuring peace. Excellencies, The constitution of Bangladesh upholds the values of peace, harmony, solidarity, and equality. Guided by these principles, our government has taken a whole of society approach to promote a culture of peace with youth at the center. Most recently, in July, August, 2024, Bangladesh witnessed a powerful youth-led uprising against discrimination. Through political transformation, this movement demonstrated the courage and commitment of our young people to justice, equality, and social inclusion. We are also promoting digital literacy and skills among youth to counter misinformation, online radicalization, and intolerance. Excellencies, for achieving SDG 16, peaceful, just, and inclusive societies, we propose the following recommendations. First, ensure enhanced access to inclusive and quality education that include values of peace and tolerance. Bridge the digital divide to provide equitable access to technology and safe digital spaces with special protection for children and youth. Promote responsible behavior in cyberspace and harness creative youth-led initiatives, including art, literature, et cetera. ensure participation of youth, including young women, in peacebuilding processes at national, regional, and global levels. Finally, strengthen cooperation with youth-led organizations, support their initiatives, as well as promote intercultural and interfaith dialogue. Excellencies, Bangladesh, as the pioneer of the culture of peace, reaffirms its unwavering commitment to the cause of achieving lasting peace, and stands ready to work with all partners to build a world where young people are not victims of violence and exclusion, but leaders of dialogue, solidarity and peace. I thank you.

I thank the distinguished representative of Bangladesh. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of Turkey, who will speak on behalf of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation. After that, you'll be Venezuela.

Mr. President, I have the honor to deliver this statement on behalf of the member states of the Organization of Islamic Cooperation in my capacity as chair of the group. Mr. President, we thank you for convening this high-level forum, which demonstrates our collective awareness of the importance of durable peace and security all over the world. It is also gratifying to note that the theme of this session focuses on the role of the youth and future generations in fostering the culture of peace in a world that is constrained by political conflicts and sustainable socioeconomic development. There is no doubt that the guiding principles of the Declaration on Future Generations have prioritized issues of maintenance of international peace and security. the role of the youth has become very relevant in various ways. Importance of intergenerational solidarity and lay along cannot be overemphasized. This is considering the need to address such challenges as the impact of climate change, promotion of ethical use of science and technology and innovation, empowerment of women and girls, and the need to eliminate racism, racial discrimination, and religious intolerance, among others. To this end, we express our commitment to promoting international peace and security anchored on the central role of multilateralism, as well as the role of the UN and regional organizations in the peaceful resolution of conflicts, with emphasis on conflict prevention and peacebuilding. In this regard, we call for resolution of the lingering political conflicts on the world stage, foremost of which is the restoration of the inalienable rights of the Palestinian people. Accordingly, and in the face of the ongoing carnage, famine and starvation in Gaza, we reiterate our call on the UN for an immediate ceasefire in Gaza and elsewhere in occupied Palestinian territory, including an early delivery of humanitarian supplies at scale to the embattled people of Gaza and Palestine. Furthermore, we submit that elimination of racism and religious intolerance can address the root cause of many international conflicts, thereby paving the way for the socioeconomic recovery necessary for the attainment of SDGs. In this regard, we express our commitment to the implementation of the UN General Assembly resolution on measures to combat Islamophobia as well as the achievements of the UN Alliance of Civilizations on promoting interreligious dialogue. Accordingly, we also express our commitment to the implementation of the provisions of General Assembly Resolution 68/127 adopted at 18 December 2013, which condemned violent extremism, stressing that violent extremism in all its forms and manifestations cannot and should not be associated with any religion, nationality, civilization or ethnic group. We welcome appointment of UN Alliance of Civilizations High Representative Mr. Moratinos as the UN Special Envoy to Combat Islamophobia, which we believe will give new impetus to new international efforts to combat this scourge. Similarly, we commend implementation of the OIC Youth Strategy and OIC Plan of Action for Advancement of Women, including activities of OIC institutions in the area of youth and women empowerment. We welcome recent organization of various youth and women-focused programs in collaboration with UN agencies, including youth and women economic empowerment, volunteering, and technological capacity building programs. I thank you again.

I thank the distinguished representative of Turkey. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative of the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela, who will speak on behalf of the Group of Friends in Defense of the Charter of the UN. After that, it will be Kyrgyzstan.

Mr. President, the Bolivarian Republic of Venezuela has the honour to take the floor on behalf of the Group of Friends in Defence of the Charter of the United Nations, the Member States of which believe the culture of peace is synonymous with the development of friendly relations between nations based on the principle of self-determination as well as the sovereignty of our peoples, their economic and social development on an equal footing, the realisation of human rights without any form of distinction, as well as the non-politicisation, non-instrumentalisation and non-imposition of double standards of any form, social justice, health and education for all, non-interference in internal affairs, respect for cultural diversity and belief in a world based on the values that inspired the establishment of the UN 80 years ago now, which are now currently in being jeopardised. In this context, we take this opportunity to reiterate our firm rejection of any hegemonic and unilateral policies that affect international peace and security in a clear attempt to threaten the principles and purposes enshrined in the Charter of the United Nations. as well as ongoing efforts towards the democratisation of international relations and the strengthening of multilateralism and of a multipolar system based, among other things, on mutual respect for the sovereignty and territorial integrity of states, as well as on respect for the principle of equal rights and the self determination of peoples, for the rule of law, diplomacy, political dialogue, tolerance, peaceful coexistence. respect for cultural diversity, inclusiveness, a culture of peace and non violence and due consideration for existing differences, all of which are essential for constructively and effectively working together on issues of common interest and concern. The culture of peace is based, among other things, on the sovereign equality of states, who are the international actors par excellence in the promotion of dialogue and cooperation among nations. For this reason, the repeal of any unilateral coercive economic or political measure is an urgent demand that cannot be postponed any longer. Since these measures affect the individual and collective rights of millions of people, they increase poverty and inequality, restrict access to essential goods and services, and foster perpetual conflict in contravention of the very tenets contained in the founding charter of our organization. It is an active call that we reiterate today once again as part of our permanent commitment to achieve a true culture of peace that is for all a reality. since otherwise it will never be a reality for anyone.
